--- title: "Meet Python: understand and run your first script" description: "For experienced frontend engineers new to Python: understand a few lines, run them locally, make changes, diagnose failures, and write a small script independently before building a full project." --- import { getFirstScriptExample } from '@/lib/js2py-examples' ## 1. Cross one learning boundary at a time You already organize frontend projects, write JavaScript, and integrate APIs. You do not need another introduction to programming itself. That experience does not, however, automatically explain Python's names, syntax, or execution model, and it does not imply that you have implemented a backend. This chapter therefore does **not** begin by scaffolding a complete Python project. Its smaller but substantive goal is to **create a Python file, explain every line, run and modify it, and repair an error you deliberately introduce**. Later chapters build language knowledge, files and modules, testing and environments, then HTTP, FastAPI, databases, and deployment. The destination is unchanged; its requirements simply do not become prerequisites for starting. ### Prerequisites, outcomes, and exclusions | Item | This chapter's contract | | --- | --- | | Prior knowledge | Using an editor and terminal; the general JS ideas of assignment, strings, and function calls | | New knowledge | Python names versus strings, assignment, calling `print`, sequential execution, running a `.py` file, and locating simple errors | | Independent outcome | Write a similarly small script without the answer, predict its output, and explain and fix a failure | | Not yet required | `import`, defining functions, reading JSON files, virtual-environment mechanisms, lockfiles, pytest, entry guards, or API servers | These excluded subjects have not been removed from the curriculum. They will receive full treatment after their prerequisites. **Exercises and exit checks in this chapter will not quietly require them.** ## 2. Understand three lines before dealing with installation Do not run anything yet or open a collection of configuration files. This is the complete program, saved as `first_steps.py`: {getFirstScriptExample('first_steps.py')} It is expected to print two lines: ```text Hello! Python ``` “Expected” matters: explain the result from the code first, then run it to check your prediction. A terminal without errors is not sufficient evidence of understanding. ### 2.1 `course = "Python"`: assign a value to a name `"Python"` is a string literal representing text. Its surrounding quotes are source-code syntax, not part of the text itself. `course` is the name we chose. After the assignment executes, later code can use this name to retrieve the corresponding value. This assignment does not start with `let`, `const`, or `var`. First establish the observable behavior: after assignment, `course` can be read; a different spelling is a different name. Mutable objects, copying, and scope are not prerequisites here. Subsequent chapters give those topics their own examples. ### 2.2 `print("Hello!")`: call an existing function `print` is a Python built-in function; this example does not need to import it. Parentheses perform a call, and `"Hello!"` is the supplied content. Here it writes that text to standard output, visible in the terminal during normal local execution, followed by a newline. **Calling an existing function** does not require **learning how to define your own function immediately**. Your understanding of JS calls helps; the new task is to understand this particular Python call. ### 2.3 `print(course)`: retrieve the value, then output it There are no quotes around `course`. Python looks up that name's value and passes the value to `print`. The result is `Python`, not `course`. The distinction can be checked independently: ```python course = "Python" print(course) print("course") ``` Expected result: ```text Python course ``` The second line reads a name; the third directly uses a literal. Similar-looking text in an editor does not necessarily mean the same thing to Python. ### 2.4 Trace execution instead of memorizing output | Position | What happens | New output | | --- | --- | --- | | Line 1 | The name `course` receives the value `"Python"` | None | | Line 2 | `print` is called with `"Hello!"` | `Hello!` | | Line 3 | The value of `course` is retrieved and passed to `print` | `Python` | Saving an assignment does not automatically display its value. We are executing a script file and explicitly printing what we want to observe. Do not transfer the browser developer console's interactive feedback directly to file execution. Blank lines can separate code and produce no output. Outside a string, `#` can start a line comment. The last line below is a note for the reader: ```python course = "Python" print(course) # This comment does not print anything. ``` ## 3. Use JS experience without erasing differences This comparison is for reading syntax. The required execution work happens in your local terminal, not in the webpage editor's runtime. ```javascript !! js const name = "Python"; console.log(name); ``` ```python !! py name = "Python" print(name) ``` Both print `Python` in this example. That does not make `const` equivalent to Python assignment or make every feature of `console.log` and `print` identical. A Python name can be assigned a new value later. Observe that behavior first: ```python course = "Python" print(course) course = "FastAPI" print(course) ``` Output: ```text Python FastAPI ``` The first output occurs before reassignment. A later assignment does not go back and change text already printed. These are ordinary strings: **writing `"FastAPI"` does not install a framework or start a server.** ## 4. What executes a `.py` file? In frontend development, an editor changes files while a browser or a runtime such as Node.js executes code. Distinguish these responsibilities for Python too: - **Editor:** creates, changes, and saves source. Syntax highlighting does not mean execution happened. - **Python language:** defines what these statements mean and how they are written. - **Python interpreter:** the program that reads and executes the code. The local course uses CPython, one implementation of Python. - **Terminal:** lets you issue startup commands and see output or errors. Shell commands are not Python source. The minimal sequence is: ```text Save first_steps.py ↓ Start the Python interpreter in the terminal and name the file ↓ The interpreter reads the file, checks syntax, then executes it ↓ Observe output or an error in the terminal ``` `.py` is the conventional extension for Python source. Renaming a JavaScript file to that extension does not translate its contents into Python. Some documentation shows an interactive Python session with a `>>>` prompt. That prompt is not source to paste into your file. This chapter consistently runs files rather than switching between execution modes. ## 5. Prepare only what this chapter needs The course uses **CPython 3.13** as its teaching baseline, not as a claim about the latest release. This script has no third-party Python dependencies and needs neither project configuration nor FastAPI. We use **uv to obtain and select the interpreter**, reducing differences between machines. Here it is a running tool: understand each command's purpose without learning the full dependency-management workflow. If uv already works, skip its installation. ### 5.1 Install and check uv Verify installation commands against the [official uv installation guide](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/). The following commands fetch and execute an official installer. Follow your organization's software policies on managed devices; do not apply this pattern to an untrusted address. **macOS / Linux terminal:** ```bash curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh ``` **Windows PowerShell:** ```powershell powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex" ``` After installation, open a new terminal and run: ```bash uv --version ``` A uv version shows that the new terminal can find the tool. If the command is still missing, follow the installer output and check your terminal/path setup. Python source has not started executing, so editing it will not fix this failure. ### 5.2 Obtain and identify the interpreter Run these lines in the terminal, not inside a `.py` file: ```bash uv python install 3.13 uv run --no-project --python 3.13 python --version ``` The first prepares Python 3.13 and can reuse an existing installation. The second selects that interpreter and asks it for its version. Expect a result beginning with `Python 3.13.`; the patch number may differ. Initial installation may require network downloads. Download progress and uv diagnostics come from the tool, not from your program. Once installed, this particular script performs no network requests. ### 5.3 Create an ordinary practice folder From a location where you keep exercises, run: ```bash mkdir js2py-first-steps cd js2py-first-steps ``` This creates and enters a folder; **it does not scaffold an application**. If it already exists from an earlier session, enter it without deleting and recreating it. Open that folder in your editor, create `first_steps.py`, enter the three lines from section 2, and save. Make sure it was not saved as `first_steps.py.txt`, particularly on systems that hide filename extensions. Alternatively, [download the chapter files](/learning-assets/js2py/u00-first-script.zip), extract them, and open a terminal in the resulting `u00-first-script` folder. Writing and downloading are two ways to obtain the same file, not two required tasks. Downloading does not replace understanding. Leave the `solutions` folder closed until you attempt the independent exercise. ## 6. Run the file and understand the command With `first_steps.py` in the terminal's current directory, run: ```bash uv run --no-project --python 3.13 python first_steps.py ``` Read the command in parts: | Part | Role here | | --- | --- | | `uv run` | Start a command through uv | | `--no-project` | Do not use a uv project in the current or parent directories as the execution context | | `--python 3.13` | Select a Python 3.13 interpreter | | `python` | The program to run is the Python interpreter | | `first_steps.py` | The file for that interpreter, located relative to the terminal's current directory | This is not a parameter table to memorize. A fixed path avoids ambiguity about which Python your machine selects. **Do not run `uv init`, create a lockfile, or install a test framework for this lesson.** A later engineering chapter will explain why environments and dependencies need isolation. Normal program output: ```text Hello! Python ``` Next, change the first line's `"Python"` to `"FastAPI"`, **save**, and run the same command again. The second output line changes; the first remains `Hello!`. Restore the original file afterward. If nothing changes, compare three things: the file saved by the editor, the terminal's current directory, and the file named in the command. Do not immediately reinstall Python; you may be editing and executing different files. ## 7. Two reversible failure experiments Make a backup copy of `first_steps.py` inside this practice folder. Change one thing at a time, observe the result, and restore it before the next experiment. Leave other projects alone. ### 7.1 Misspelled name: valid syntax, failed lookup during execution Change only `course` in the last line to `cours`: ```python expected-error=NameError course = "Python" print("Hello!") print(cours) ``` You will see `Hello!`, followed by an error containing `NameError`. The first two lines have executed. Execution cannot proceed normally when the third line tries to retrieve a name that has not been assigned. Read the error type and message at the end, find your own filename and line number above it, then inspect that source line. `course` and `cours` are different names. Fix the spelling; do not install a package named `cours`. You do not need to memorize every traceback field. Locate your own file and understand this failure's immediate cause. After repairing it, rerun and check that both normal output lines return. ### 7.2 Missing quote: the file cannot be parsed before execution Remove the closing double quote on the first line: ```python expected-error=SyntaxError course = "Python print("Hello!") print(course) ``` This produces `SyntaxError`, and neither `print` in the file executes. The interpreter finds invalid syntax before it starts executing the statements. Exact wording and caret placement can vary between patch versions. You do not need to memorize them. Restore the quote, save, and rerun to complete the experiment. ### 7.3 Identify the failing layer first | Symptom | Check first | Do not start by | | --- | --- | --- | | `uv` command not found | Installation and whether a new terminal can find it | Editing Python business logic | | Cannot open `first_steps.py` | Directory, filename, and accidental `.txt` extension | Installing a Python package | | `SyntaxError` | Highlighted source, including quotes and parentheses | Switching frameworks | | `NameError` | Whether that name was assigned and spelled consistently | Reinstalling the environment | | Old output remains | Saved file and the actual file being executed | Assuming program output is a cache problem | This is a guide to these experiments, not an exhaustive explanation of every error with the same name. Preserve the actual command and message rather than guessing from an error type alone. ## 8. Exercises: explain, modify, and write independently ### Exercise 1: predict before executing Without running it, write down the three output lines and explain why a later assignment cannot change text that was already printed. ```python topic = "Python" print(topic) topic = "FastAPI" print("topic") print(topic) ```
Read the explanation after your attempt ```text Python topic FastAPI ``` The first call reads the old value, the second prints the literal `"topic"`, and the third reads the reassigned value. Previously printed terminal text is not a frontend component that automatically updates when a name changes.
### Exercise 2: change one thing Starting from the original `first_steps.py`, change only the last line to `print("course")`. Predict both output lines, save and verify, then restore the original. Explain why this no longer retrieves the value assigned on the first line. Go beyond “the quotes make it different”: what does the quoted content represent, and what would the interpreter do without quotes?
Check the result after your attempt The lines are `Hello!` and `course`. The final call directly receives a string literal, not a value obtained through a name. Restoring `print(course)` makes it read that assigned value again.
### Exercise 3: create another file independently Create `about_me.py` in the same folder. Follow these requirements without copying the answer: 1. Assign `"Python"` to the name `subject`. 2. Print `My next skill:`, then the current value of `subject`. 3. Reassign the same name to `"FastAPI"`, then print its new value. Do not hard-code all three output lines to bypass reading and reassigning the name. No imports, loops, custom functions, or additional tools are needed. Run: ```bash uv run --no-project --python 3.13 python about_me.py ``` Expected output: ```text My next skill: Python FastAPI ```
See a reference implementation after trying independently {getFirstScriptExample('solutions/about_me.py')} There can be other valid implementations, but assignment, lookup, and reassignment must actually occur. Change the first assigned value to `"Python basics"`: only the second output line should change. Explaining this variation provides better evidence of understanding than matching the reference visually.
## 9. When are you ready to continue? - [ ] Distinguish terminal commands from Python source and identify what executes the source. - [ ] Create and run a `.py` file in an ordinary folder, not only from a download. - [ ] Explain names, quoted strings, assignment, and `print` in this example. - [ ] Predict and verify output before and after reassignment. - [ ] Write `about_me.py` and a variation independently rather than hard-coding all output. - [ ] Introduce and repair one of this chapter's failures, locating the file, position, and cause. **Passing pytest, explaining four configuration files, and reconstructing a complete application are not exit requirements.** Those skills have their own learning stages. When pausing, leave a recovery note: ```text Current practice folder: Last saved and executed file: Last successful command and output: A line I cannot yet explain: The first small action for my next session: ``` Next time, run that file, explain each line aloud, then try one small variation. There is no daily streak requirement and no need to reinstall everything after a break. ## 10. What comes next, and where to look things up The new route next develops **names, values, and basic operations**, followed by separate chapters on containers, control flow, functions, exceptions, modules, and files. Small practical programs continue throughout; you do not wait through a long theory-only phase. > **Rewrite status (2026-09-23):** This chapter follows the new small-script contract. [The current chapter 01](/en/docs/js2py/module-01-syntax-comparison) remains the older combined chapter, not the new single-topic lesson. Its assignment and basic-data-type sections can be read first; the later topics are not hidden prerequisites omitted from this chapter. Subsequent lessons will be rewritten one at a time. Consult official references for a specific question rather than reading their entire sites before starting: - Basic expressions and interaction: [Python 3.13 tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3.13/tutorial/introduction.html). - Complete parameters and behavior of `print`: [Python built-ins](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/functions.html#print). This lesson uses only its simplest form. - Syntax errors versus execution-time exceptions: [Python errors and exceptions](https://docs.python.org/3.13/tutorial/errors.html). Full exception handling comes later. - The execution command: [uv script guide](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/scripts/). This dependency-free script does not need a uv project first.

intro_alignment.instructions: Does the actual lesson satisfy the approved introductory learning contract for this reader? Choose the best overall disposition.

criteria.ALIGNED: The required scope is a comprehensible small script rather than premature independent engineering; core contract is met.
